items.title: [ArchDaily] Lina Bo Bardi and Popular Making: Craft and Accessibility in Design
items.content_html: In an era where digital fabrication and automation are increasingly present in architectural practice, manual craft is often seen as a luxury item—restricted to high-end projects whose clients can afford extended deadlines and collaborative processes requiring constant dialogue with artisans. This scenario might have sounded contradictory a few decades ago, when Lina Bo Bardi warned that a process of "deculturalization" was underway and that a critical assessment of "popular" Brazilian civilization was urgently needed to confront totalizing universalisms and *folklore*—the latter viewed by her as an instrument of state alienation designed to neutralize the subversive and transformative character of popular culture:

items.title: [ArchDaily] Santa Cruz School Kindergarten / Andrade Morettin Arquitetos Associados
items.content_html: The courtyard-school concept guides the project, treating the space itself as a third educator and play as an essential pillar of the architecture. In this design, the building acts as an acoustic barrier against urban noise, turning primarily inward to create a welcoming and safe environment. The Central Courtyard emerges as the heart of the project and the main gathering space, organizing the ground-floor classrooms to foster interaction among different age groups.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Katūvu Hut / HUT atelier d'architecture
items.content_html: The KATŪVU hut is situated on the outskirts of the hamlet of Les Prières, on the road to the Col de Tamié, which separates the departments of Savoie and Haute-Savoie. The site, situated on the edge of the forest, slopes gently toward the southwest, naturally drawing the eye toward the summit of the pass and Tamié Abbey, a Cistercian monastery founded in the 12th century. The vast surrounding landscape exudes a unique atmosphere, inviting a sense of elevation. Physical, first of all, through the natural ascent toward the pass, itself framed by the first imposing peaks of the Bauges massif. Spiritual, secondly, through the presence of a major religious site and localities with symbolic place names.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Country House in Boladala Village / ARC Architects
items.content_html: The country house is located on the shore of the Charvak Reservoir, an artificial lake surrounded by mountains, approximately 80 km from Tashkent. The village of Boladala is one of the more remote settlements along the reservoir, largely untouched by tourism. The house is located on the edge of the village, with open views of the lake and surrounding mountains.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Floral Pavilion / genarchitects
items.content_html: "Floral Pavilion" and the small railway station are two buildings located not far from one another in Tangshan, Jiangning District, Nanjing. The small train forms part of the park's transportation system, and the platform we designed is one of many stations along the route. The rest pavilions, meanwhile, provide visitors with toilets, places to rest, and refreshments. There are several of them throughout the park, each with a different theme. The theme of the "Floral Pavilion" is garden plants.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The long and beautiful story of Native American graphic design
items.content_html:
Brian Johnson, a member of the Monacan Indian Nation, is painting the field of graphic design red, with his new book, Designed to Be Red: Native & Indigenous Graphic Works, published on September 15 by DelMonico Books. The book contributes to the larger project of decolonizing design. Showing more than 200 years of Native American graphic works from makers across 144 distinct nations, tribes, bands, and Indigenous cultural and language groups, the book dismantles the myth of design as something that happened in Europe in the 1800s.

Sparked by a request to give a lecture on Native American posters by the New York City gallery Poster House, Johnson carried out his project of “cultural sovereignty” for three years. His Native American heritage and career as a designer, curator, and partner at the design studio Polymode earned the trust from the Native and Indigenous makers and guiding Aunties who contributed to the book.

In a two-hour Zoom interview, which has been edited for brevity and clarity, I sat down with Johnson to discuss the significance of this project for Native American and Indigenous makers and why non-Native people still need to be reminded to “Put Native First.”   

Fast Company: Would you please explain the title of your book, Designed to Be Red: Native & Indigenous Graphic Works?

Brian Johnson: The title stems from this idea that everything is by design. And that Native Americans were designed [by colonization] to be “red.” This idea where we have been othered, classified, and made a taxonomy. We are in the past. We are imagined. I think dad jokes are the best thing ever because wordplay is really important to me. I think it is funny. I think it lets your guard down. That’s also a very Native trait. And so, to be red also means to be R-E-A-D, to be read like a book, to be read like a story, to be read to filth. I loved the play on words. To take a word, red, that is used as a weapon and then to flip it and show it was also designed to be read.

Tell me what is your authorial (i.e. both author and authority) relationship to the book?

First, I am Native American. I come from the Monacan Indian Nation, whose ancestral lands are in central Virginia: Lynchburg, Richmond, Charlottesville, and the Shenandoah Valley. Being proud of where I come from has always been one of the deepest parts of me. The Monacan Indian Nation finally got federal recognition in 2018 by the United States government. To some people, unless you have a certain level of recognition, whether it be state or federal, you are not allowed to be that thing.

I went to RISD [Rhode Island School of Design], where I got a great education. I have been in the design world now for 25-plus years. I am a partner at Polymode. I work really hard to uplift marginalized voices. I started BIPOC Design History with Silas Munro. I am here to really show that people of color have been making, doing, striving, and surviving in beautiful waves for eons.

But it’s not just me, I invited other Native American scholars and designers to be in conversation with me: Dr. Jessica Moore Harjo (Otoe-Missouria, Osage, Pawnee, and Sac & Fox Nations), Monique Ortman (Cherokee Nation), Jackson Polys (Tlingit), Sadie Red Wing (Spirit Lake Dakota/Cheyenne River Lakota), Kathleen Sleboda (Nlaka’pamux/Coldwater Indian Band), and Leo Vicenti (Jicarilla Apache Nation).

Would you talk about your process of collecting and curating the over 100 graphic works for the book?

First, it was finding the works. In the Western design thinking, this follows the modernist timeline. From Native viewpoints, this is not the way we conceptualize the world. We think about everything as a web. It is all enmeshed together.

And so, I started by asking, “Where are the pieces that I know?” I knew about Akwesasne Notes, the newspaper that was key for the American Indian Movement, and those posters. As a child of the early ‘80s, I grew up in schools that had the “Hang in There” or “Soar with the Eagles” posters. I grew up remembering the Crying Native ad, with old Iron Eyes Cody, the pretendian. I also knew the extractive negative works that were in the common understanding of the things called Native.

Then once I found hundreds of works, I asked, “What are the stories behind them?” And I had to cold-call people, get on Facebook and Instagram, literally call up the Aunties and email people that I had never met and tell my story 5,000 times.

Then there is all the stuff you’re taught from a higher education standpoint. Go to an archive, open up the flat file, look through it, find what you need. But nine times out of 10, they weren’t documented or attributed correctly. It said “unknown.” That is not true. These are “maker once known.” These individuals were erased.

What are images that you knew you wanted to include in the book from the beginning?

The first image was The Shrine to Hypocrisy by Akwesasne Notes. It is a poster of Mount Rushmore and Chief Sitting Bull’s head rising behind the American presidents that were bastardly carved into those sacred mountains. Everyone knows what Mount Rushmore is because of the American myth behind it. But that poster was saying, “Remember, your ancestors never gave away or sold that land.” It’s this dichotomy between how everyone sees and knows it.

The other one is something closer to me, and that is the Powhatan’s Mantle. It is this large deer skin that has all of these shells so delicately sewn onto it. It has a human, two deer, and all of these circles that represent the different tribes or people that are all bound together in what is now called the Powhatan Confederacy. That object has deep meaning to me, even though I am not from that Native lineage, those people were from nearby lands. I knew of that object and how it was “given” as a gift to the King of England, where it now still sits.

You end the book with a call to action. What are those things that people should be doing to support the cultural sovereignty of Native American graphic works?

Yes, in the book there is an explicit call to action where people can understand “What can I do next?” for young Natives, for older Natives, for students, for non-Natives, for educators. Some of those things are: Try to decolonize what you’re teaching. Try to expand and find more things. Question the authority of what you’ve been shown. Ask the same questions from a different terminology. Sometimes sit down and let other Native people speak. The main point is that you have to slow down the idea of capitalism and the machine to do the real work to reestablish what has been destroyed—community connection and the value between human beings.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Guangnan Gospel Hall Renewal / TouchGrass Architecture
items.content_html: Built in 1930 and dedicated in 1932, Guangnan Gospel Hall is the only timber church in Guangxi. Led by Dong pastor Shi Zhengang, villagers built it in local fir using traditional chuandou framing beneath a hipped roof, grounding an imported faith in local building traditions. Over nearly a century, the Gospel Hall has served as a place of worship, village committee office, elders' activity room, and primary school classroom. Each use left traces. By 2025, the timber structure had severely deteriorated: members were widely decayed, the frame had settled unevenly with localized collapse, and the enclosure no longer protected the interior from wind and rain.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Timbercraft: Lost Tectonics from East Asia
items.content_html:
At a time when timber is again reshaping architectural practice, Timbercraft: Lost Tectonics from East Asia revisits the enduring legacy of traditional East Asian construction. Spanning more than 1,400 years, the book examines nine landmark buildings in China, Japan, and Korea, tracing the evolution of sophisticated timber systems through interlocking components, bracket complexes, and intricate joinery.

Written by architect and researcher Jae K Kim, Timbercraft makes this complex body of knowledge accessible through original analytical drawings, section perspectives, exploded axonometric views, and assembly studies. items.title: [ArchDaily] Donald Judd’s Artillery Sheds in Texas to Undergo Major Restoration
items.content_html: The Chinati Foundation has announced plans to restore the Artillery Sheds in Marfa, Texas, the former military buildings adapted by artist Donald Judd to house his 100 untitled works in mill aluminum, created between 1982 and 1986. Led by architect Troy Schaum of Schaum Architects, the multi-year preservation project is being developed with the Getty Conservation Institute and will address the historic buildings' envelope, accessibility, environmental performance, and landscape while preserving Judd's site-specific installation. The project follows the Artillery Sheds' inclusion in the National Register of Historic Places in 2025 as part of the expanded Donald Judd Historic District.

items.title: [ArchDaily] OMA/AMO and OPEN Architecture Design Opening Exhibitions for Powerhouse Parramatta in Sydney, Australia
items.content_html: Powerhouse Parramatta, a new museum and cultural institution on the banks of the Parramatta River in Western Sydney, Australia, will open to the public on Saturday, November 7, 2026. The 30,000-square-meter building has been designed by Franco-Japanese firm Moreau Kusunoki as lead designer, with Australian firm Genton as local architect and Arup as engineer. Moreau Kusunoki won the design competition for the project in 2019, with completion initially planned for 2025. Powerhouse Parramatta is the first state cultural organization located in Western Sydney, a region whose population includes communities from more than 170 countries. At opening, the museum will present five exhibitions.

items.title: [ArchDaily] HUB UCC. Universidad Católica de Córdoba Innovation Space / BLT Arquitectos
items.content_html: The Universidad Católica de Córdoba operates on a campus that, following the traditional format, originally assigned a building to each academic unit or field of study. In a contemporary world that demands interdisciplinary research and design dynamics, architecture must transcend fragmentation to enhance collective life and foster social cohesion within the academic community. This requires more flexible spaces that, rather than functioning as isolated compartments, encourage the intersection of disciplines and ideas to foster innovation and the development of new projects. The architecture of the hub makes room for what is yet unknown, for innovation, creation, and the materialization of ideas, and for the interdisciplinary convergence of the university community.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Cinema Studio Namibe: Reviving a Tropical Modernist Icon in Angola
items.content_html: What sustains the purpose of architecture that has never been occupied? For decades, this was the question surrounding the Namibe Cinema-Studio, built on the coast of Angola in 1973. Conceived as a film screening venue, the building remained closed and abandoned, never fulfilling the role for which it was created. Yet it withstood the passage of time, becoming an icon of the Angolan landscape and architecture, until finally screening its first film nearly fifty years later.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Raw & Warm Residence / Habitat Architects
items.content_html: Raw & Warm was conceived as a residential laboratory for an art collector—a home where architecture, art, and daily life could coexist without competing for attention. Rather than concealing the original structure, the design preserves the exposed concrete ceiling and its irregular texture, allowing the building's raw character to become the starting point of the spatial narrative.

items.title: [ArchDaily] The Threshold House / Madras Spaces
items.content_html: Located in V. Thuraiyur, near Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu, this 1000 sq.ft farmhouse by Madras Spaces is conceived as a quiet return to a lost native landscape. Set amidst agricultural fields and far removed from urban noise, the project responds to a tight site, limited resources, and a brief rooted more in memory and belonging than in program.
